posts.quote: The font on everything got smaller around the same time my arms got shorter. That can't be a coincidence.
posts.caption: Last week I read the back of a cereal box from the other side of the kitchen. The cereal was fine. My arms were the problem. I held the box out until my elbows locked, turned it toward the window, tilted it, and still got nothing but a gray smudge where the ingredients should be. I considered the possibility that every printer agreed to shrink the type on the same Tuesday. I put the box back in the cupboard and ate the cereal anyway, because guessing has never once let me down. I'm told there are vitamins in there.
posts.first: My pharmacy now slides a little magnifying card across the counter with my prescriptions. Nobody says anything about it. It just appears, like a quiet intervention. I keep it in my purse next to the receipts I also can't read.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding a cereal box at full arm's length and squinting at it in a bright kitchen, a glass of red wine on the counter. Text at the top reads: The font on everything got smaller around the same time my arms got shorter. That can't be a coincidence.

posts.quote: My mother ate dinner at 4:30 and I judged her. Today I checked whether the restaurant would take us at 4:15.
posts.caption: She'd call it early bird. I call it the only reasonable time to be seated. The bread arrives while the parking lot is still empty.
posts.first: Last Friday we were first through the door at 4:20. The hostess handed us menus like she'd been expecting us for years. We ordered, ate, and were home before the news came on. I felt wonderful about it. My mother would have loved that hostess.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun standing at a restaurant host stand with an empty dining room behind her and a wall clock reading quarter past four. Text in the speech bubble reads: My mother ate dinner at 4:30 and I judged her. Today I checked whether the restaurant would take us at 4:15.

posts.quote: I caught myself getting genuinely excited about a gutter guard sale. Younger me is horrified. Current me bought two.
posts.caption: It started with a flyer in the mail. The flyer said gutter guards were forty percent off through Sunday, and I read it twice standing at the mailbox, with a feeling I haven't had since a concert in 1992. I called my sister, who wasn't impressed. I called my neighbor, who has opinions about downspouts and shared all of them. By Saturday I had a ladder, a plan, and a level of focus I've never brought to a tax form. The gutters are spotless. I'm not proud, but I'm not ashamed either.
posts.first: My neighbor stopped by afterward and tapped the gutter with a knuckle like he was checking a melon. He nodded once and left. It was the nicest compliment anyone has paid me all year. I've been walking a little taller in the driveway ever since.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun, beaming and holding up a sale flyer in one hand and a glass of red wine in the other against a plain cream background. Text beside her reads: I caught myself getting genuinely excited about a gutter guard sale. Younger me is horrified. Current me bought two.

posts.quote: I turned my head too fast to check a noise and pulled a muscle. The noise was the dishwasher.
posts.caption: The house made a sound. I assumed the worst and moved like a cat. It was a dishwasher doing exactly its job. My neck has since filed a complaint.
posts.first: That was Tuesday. It's now Thursday and I'm still turning my whole torso to look at things, like a person in a museum. The heating pad is helping. The dishwasher has not apologized.
posts.alt: Comic panel illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun wincing and holding her neck in a kitchen where a dishwasher sits quietly behind her, a glass of red wine on the counter. Text at the top reads: I turned my head too fast to check a noise. Text at the bottom reads: And pulled a muscle. The noise was the dishwasher.

posts.quote: There is a particular peace in a clean kitchen at 9 p.m. with nothing left to do and nowhere left to be.
posts.first: I wiped down the counter, turned off the overhead light, and left only the small lamp over the stove on. Eleven quiet minutes and nothing on the list. I counted it as a day well finished and went to bed with a glass of water and a book I've been rereading for months.

posts.quote: I've been on hold with the cable company so long I know the hold music better than my own ringtone.
posts.caption: Forty-one minutes in, I was no longer on hold. I was a regular. The song loops every ninety seconds, and a woman's voice comes on every third loop to say my call is important. I've started to believe her, because nobody puts that much effort into a saxophone solo otherwise. I did a load of laundry on speaker. I watered the plants. I ate a clementine, slowly. When a real person finally picked up, I almost said I was just about to hang up. The issue was resolved in four minutes. The saxophone and I are still in touch.
posts.first: The man who finally answered was named Dale, and he sounded as tired as I felt. We got through the whole thing in under five minutes. Before he hung up he said thanks for waiting. I told him it was no trouble. I'd just learned all the words to the saxophone.
posts.alt: Painted illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sitting at a kitchen table with a phone on speaker beside a glass of red wine, swaying calmly with her eyes closed. Text at the top reads: I've been on hold with the cable company so long. Text at the bottom reads: I know the hold music better than my own ringtone.

posts.quote: I paid cash at the self-checkout. The machine got so confused it called over a teenager, and we both felt awkward.
posts.caption: Cash used to be the simple option. Now it's an event. Three people asked if I needed help, and one of them looked genuinely moved.
posts.first: The teenager scanned something, pressed something, and the drawer popped open with a noise I hadn't heard in ten years. He looked at the coins like they were artifacts. I told him he was doing great. He thanked me, and I walked out feeling like I'd taught a class.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding out a few dollar bills at a grocery self-checkout kiosk while a young teenage store clerk in a green apron looks puzzled at the screen. Text at the top reads: I paid cash at the self-checkout. The machine got so confused it called over a teenager, and we both felt awkward.

posts.quote: My mother kept every plastic bag inside a bigger plastic bag. I now have a bag of bags, and a drawer for the bag of bags.
posts.caption: There is a bag in my pantry that holds every plastic bag I have ever been handed. I did not decide to start it. It started itself, sometime around 2019, and now there is a drawer for the overflow. Last week I stood there pulling bags out one at a time, looking for a specific small one, and found a receipt from a hardware store that closed in 2011. My mother would have been proud. She would also have asked why I only had that many. I put everything back exactly as I found it. You never know when you will need nine.
posts.first: My mother folded hers into tight little triangles, like a flag. I never learned the fold, so I stuff. On Tuesday I needed one bag for a wet umbrella and found three in the car, four in my purse, and none in the drawer.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman in her early 50s with a messy auburn bun, grey streaks and glasses on her forehead, wearing an olive vest over a striped shirt. She holds up a big clear plastic bag stuffed with more plastic bags beside an open kitchen drawer overflowing with bags. Text at the top reads: My mother kept every plastic bag inside a bigger plastic bag. I now have a bag of bags, and a drawer for the bag of bags.

posts.quote: I turned off the news and put on a documentary about lighthouse keepers. My blood pressure sent a thank-you card.
posts.caption: Two hours of lighthouse keeper history, narrated by a man who sounds like warm oatmeal. Nothing exploded. Nobody yelled.
posts.first: I didn't plan to watch the whole thing. By the credits I knew how to trim a wick and what a fog signal meant in 1890. It's the calmest evening I've had in months, and I'm putting another one on tomorrow.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a relaxed woman with a messy grey-streaked bun curled up on a couch under a blanket with a glass of red wine, watching a television showing a lighthouse on a rocky coast at dusk. Text at the top reads: I turned off the news and put on a documentary about lighthouse keepers. My blood pressure sent a thank-you card.

posts.quote: I raked for two hours. The wind put it all back in eleven minutes. We both took it personally.
posts.caption: The yard looked perfect for roughly one afternoon. I raked until my shoulders gave a stern warning, bagged six sacks, and stood on the porch admiring the lawn like a proud landowner. At 4:10 the wind showed up. By 4:21 the leaves were back, along with some new ones I'm sure came from another neighborhood. I went inside and watched from the window. A single oak leaf tumbled across the grass as if it had never heard of me. I'm choosing to believe the wind and I have a rivalry that makes us both better. Tomorrow, round two.
posts.first: My neighbor three doors down uses a leaf blower and finishes in fifteen minutes. He's never once looked as defeated as I do. I've decided I prefer the rake. It makes the loss feel earned.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman in her early 50s with a messy auburn bun, grey streaks and glasses on her forehead, wearing an olive vest over a striped shirt, raking a front yard under a big oak tree while red and gold autumn leaves blow back across the lawn. Six full leaf bags stand beside her. Text at the top reads: I raked for two hours. The wind put it all back in eleven minutes. We both took it personally.

posts.quote: My grey hairs have formed a union. They stopped coming in one at a time and started arriving as a group.
posts.caption: They arrived one at a time for years. Now they come in groups, with matching posture and a sense of purpose.
posts.first: My stylist held up a section and said, wow, they're organized. I asked if she could negotiate. She offered a color. I said I'd think about it, which means I'm keeping them. They've earned a seat at the table.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun leaning toward a bathroom mirror and inspecting a bright silver strand, a glass of red wine on the sink edge. Text at the top reads: My grey hairs have formed a union. They stopped coming in one at a time and started arriving as a group.

posts.quote: The best chair in the house is the one nobody else is allowed to sit in, and everyone knows which one it is.
posts.first: In our house it's the green armchair by the window. Everyone has sat in it at some point, usually when I'm in the other room, and I always know. The cushion has a very specific dent. I've never said a word about it, and everybody understands.

posts.quote: My doctor said to drink more water. I carry a forty ounce cup everywhere. It has been to every room and never once been opened.
posts.caption: The cup has been with me for six months and I've never seen the bottom. It's a big insulated one, dark green, with a straw and a lid that clicks. I carry it from the kitchen to the car to the couch to the laundry room, and I set it down on counters like a small, loyal friend. At my last checkup the doctor asked how much water I drink in a day. I held up the cup. She asked how much of it I'd actually finished. I looked at the cup. The cup looked at me. She wrote something down, and I'd rather not know what.
posts.first: I tried a timer on my phone this week. Every hour it chimed, I took exactly two sips, felt wonderful, and put the cup down somewhere. I'm now on my third search of the house for the cup. At least the timer works.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sitting on a doctor's exam table holding a huge dark green insulated cup with a straw, with an exam room, a stethoscope on a hook and a glass of red wine on a side counter. Text in the speech bubble reads: My doctor said to drink more water. I carry a forty ounce cup everywhere. It has been to every room and never once been opened.

posts.quote: The squirrels have been burying acorns in my flowerpots since September, and they're so organized I'm starting to feel like a landlord.
posts.caption: There are two squirrels in my yard who run it like a small business. Every morning at seven they dig up the same flowerpot, hide an acorn, and pat the soil down like a pair of tiny gardeners. By noon, a third squirrel steals it and the whole thing starts over. I filled the pots with mums last month, thinking I'd got ahead of the problem. They sniffed the mums and carried on digging right beside them. I've stopped being annoyed. I pay in sunflower seeds now. It's less of a fight and more of a retainer.
posts.first: This morning I counted fourteen acorns in the porch pots. I didn't plant a single one. I'm fairly sure I'm now responsible for a food storage facility. I looked for the lease. There isn't one.
posts.alt: Painted illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sitting on a porch step holding a glass of red wine and watching a squirrel bury an acorn in a pot of orange mums, with autumn leaves around. Text at the top reads: The squirrels have been burying acorns in my flowerpots since September. Text at the bottom reads: And they're so organized I'm starting to feel like a landlord.

posts.quote: My Saturday is organized around where the sun lands on the porch chair. Everything else is negotiable.
posts.caption: The sun moves, so I move. It's the closest thing to a fitness routine I have, and I stick to it.
posts.first: By three o'clock the chair gets the sun for exactly fifty minutes. I plan around it. The dog thinks it's his chair, but he knows I started this. We share a respectful silence and one blanket.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman in her mid-50s with short mauve-pink curls, a mustard fairisle sweater and fluffy pink slippers, relaxing with her eyes closed in a wooden porch rocking chair in warm autumn sunlight, a plaid blanket over her lap, a glass of red wine beside her and a golden dog asleep at her feet. Text at the top reads: My Saturday is organized around where the sun lands on the porch chair. Everything else is negotiable.

posts.quote: I spent fifty-five minutes comparing two brands of paper towels that differ by eleven cents. I believe I did the research well.
posts.caption: I stood in the paper goods aisle for fifty-five minutes, and I'd like it noted that I finished. Brand A had 120 sheets per roll and a pattern of tiny leaves. Brand B had 112 sheets and was eleven cents cheaper per roll. I took out my phone to calculate the price per sheet and discovered my phone calculator has no feelings about leaves. A woman with a full cart went around me twice, once with a look. I chose Brand A, put it in the cart, took it out, and put it back in. Total savings: roughly nothing. Total satisfaction: surprisingly high.
posts.first: At home I discovered I already had six rolls in the pantry, behind the foil. I didn't mention this to anyone. Brand A looks great on the shelf, though. I've lined the rolls up by height. It's become a small point of pride.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding two paper towel rolls side by side and comparing them with a thoughtful frown against a plain cream background, a glass of red wine in her other hand. Text beside her reads: I spent fifty-five minutes comparing two brands of paper towels that differ by eleven cents. I believe I did the research well.
